title: Score VExUS (Venous Excess Ultrasound)
formula:
The VExUS Score is determined by the following grading system:

| Variable | Grade |
| --- | --- |
| IVC <2 cm | 0 |
| IVC ≥2 cm Doppler: normal patterns or mild abnormalities in at least one site* | 1 |
| IVC ≥2 cm Doppler: severe abnormalities in at least one site* | 2 |
| IVC ≥2 cm Doppler: severe abnormalities in at least two sites* | 3 |

*Hepatic vein, portal vein, intra-renal vein

![](https://s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/cdn-web-img.mdcalc.com/content/vexus-evidence.png)

- **Hepatic doppler** is considered mildly abnormal when the systolic (S) component is lower in magnitude than the diastolic (D) component, but still toward the liver, while it is considered severely abnormal when the S component is reversed (toward the heart).
- **Portal doppler** is considered mildly abnormal when a variation in the velocities during the cardiac cycle of 30 to <50% are observed, while it is considered severely abnormal when a variation of ≥50% is seen.
- **Intra‑renal venous doppler** is considered mildly abnormal when it is discontinuous with a systolic (S) and diastolic (D) phase, while it is considered severely abnormal when it is discontinuous with only a diastolic phase seen during the cardiac cycle.

how_to_use.why:
- Evaluation of volume overload is often difficult, and previous research has demonstrated that IVC assessment alone may be unreliable for guiding fluid tolerance.
- This tool allows for a quantitative assessment of venous congestion, which may support a congestive etiology for acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients with acute decompensated heart failure and suspected cardiorenal syndrome.
- Serial grading can help assess response to decongestion and support titration of diuretic therapy during hospitalization.
how_to_use.when:
- Utilisation chez l’adulte (≥18 ans) en cas de suspicion de surcharge volémique et de congestion veineuse dues à un syndrome cardio-rénal.
- Souvent utilisé de manière sériée (p. ex., quotidiennement) pour suivre l’évolution de la congestion veineuse pendant le traitement.
how_to_use.pearls:
- Has not been validated in patients in whom hepatic vein Doppler waveforms would be abnormal (e.g., mechanical ventilation, ventricular assist device use, tricuspid regurgitation, severe pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure).
- Interlobar renal vein waveforms may be less reliable in severe chronic kidney disease (eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73m^2^), renal transplant, or cirrhosis with portal hypertension.
- Requires ECG tracing on the ultrasound to correctly interpret Doppler waveforms.
- Although interrater reliability has been reported in several studies, the exam is operator dependent and often requires specific training to complete.
- Even with significant training, exams could not be completed in 10%–20% of patients in published studies.
- Studies show good correlation of VExUS Grade 3 with elevated right atrial pressure; distinctions between Grades 0,1, and 2 may be less clear.

next_steps.advice:
- Results from this tool may be incorporated into a patient’s overall clinical picture to guide diuresis or predict the development of postoperative AKI.
- Apply in patients who meet the original study criteria; use caution in patients with:

 - Tricuspid regurgitation.
 - Mechanical ventilation.
 - Ventricular assist devices or mechanical circulatory support.
- Reliability may be reduced in patients with chronic kidney disease (eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73m^2^) or renal transplant.
- Studies recommend serial evaluations, often at 24- to 72-hour intervals.
next_steps.critical_actions: Do not delay time-sensitive, life-saving therapies in unstable patients to perform this exam.
next_steps.management:
- **Grade ≥2 :** Envisager des diurétiques pour la décongestion veineuse.
- **Grade 0–1 :** Les patients peuvent encore bénéficier d’une diurèse ; guider le traitement en fonction du contexte clinique, de l’examen physique et des examens biologiques.

evidence:
The initial development of the VExUS Score by[Beaubien-Souligny et al. (2020)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7142196/)was conducted in 145 patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Investigators excluded patients with severe chronic kidney disease (eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73m^2^), prior renal transplant, critical preoperative state, documented preoperative AKI, and any condition that could interfere with Doppler evaluation of the portal system (e.g., cirrhosis, portal vein thrombosis). Investigators tested five grading prototypes (A–E). In a post hoc analysis, VExUS ≥2 was associated with postoperative AKI in this cohort and outperformed central venous pressure with increased specificity. Prototype C was selected as the best-performing approach for predicting postoperative AKI.

These findings were subsequently validated in several studies, including those by[Klompmaker et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40286489/),[Utrilla-Alvarez et al.](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/echo.15697), and[Bhardwaj et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7584837/)Across these studies, a grade ≥2 was associated with development of AKI, and serial assessments suggested that trends in the VExUS grade could help guide venous decongestion and track renal recovery. This was recently supported by a prospective study of critically ill patients with heart failure, in which VExUS was closely associated with right atrial pressure both before decongestion and after significant diuresis. Notably, these investigations largely involved patients with preexisting cardiac disease or high risk for cardiorenal syndrome. Collectively, they suggest that although higher VExUS grades are less common, they can effectively stratify the degree of venous congestion in this population.

In contrast, studies in more heterogeneous ICU populations have yielded less consistent results.[Andrei et al.](https://ccforum.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13054-023-04524-4)and[Magin et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10721303/)found that in patients undergoing noncardiac surgery or admitted to general ICUs, the VExUS did not predict AKI or mortality. Other studies have correlated higher VExUS grades with increased right atrial pressures and reduced diuretic efficiency. Variable performance in general ICU cohorts may reflect the multifactorial causes of AKI in multi-organ failure, where venous congestion may be only one contributor and decongestion may not address the primary driver. Further research is needed to clarify the best use of VExUS in these populations.

Two recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses have sought to further elucidate the role of VExUS in heart failure.[Chaves et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41747972/)reviewed 5 studies and found that lower VExUS grades were associated with improved in-hospital mortality (mean odds ratio 0.175).[Carsetti et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41606663/)reviewed 8 studies and found that higher grades were associated with lower measures of right ventricular function (e.g., tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion), but only among patients with known heart failure. As such, it is reasonable that VExUS may continue to be used as a marker of systemic congestion rather than that of ventricular dysfunction.

Overall, these findings indicate that VExUS is most valuable in assessing AKI risk in patients at risk for cardiorenal syndrome, with less consistent performance in general ICU populations. Some evidence also links VExUS to mortality in heart failure. Because most studies excluded patients with significant liver disease or advanced renal disease, apply the score cautiously in these groups. To our knowledge, no impact analyses or clinical practice guidelines have incorporated VExUS into routine clinical assessment.

instructions:
The derivation study used the following ultrasound/Doppler techniques:

- **IVC diameter:** Measure inner-to-inner wall in a longitudinal subxiphoid view of the intrahepatic segment, approximately 2 cm caudal to the hepatic vein confluence, using the maximal diameter over the respiratory cycle.
- **Hepatic and portal vein Doppler:** Use a mid- to posterior-axillary transthoracic window.
- **Intrarenal venous Doppler:** Use a posterior axillary approach to obtain a longitudinal kidney view, then acquire a pulsed-wave Doppler waveform at the corticomedullary junction.
- Obtain a concurrent ECG tracing to identify phases of the cardiac cycle.

See[Beaubien-Souligny et al. (2018)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30371304/)for additional detail.
